clue.text: Very obvious King acts really flustered

indicators.note: someone flustered is thrown into disorder, so the letters before it are jumbled

parts.note: Carolus Rex, the Latin royal title on old documents
the letters to be mixed, taken as printed

explanation.surface: A monarch loses his composure and his performance goes to pieces in full view of everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Really' looks like an adverb qualifying 'flustered', but its letters are fodder; the king is the two-letter CR, not K or R alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Something crystal clear is plainly evident, so the idiom is a straight synonym for an adjective meaning obvious.

clue.text: That man is wearing Wally's costume

indicators.note: what is worn sits around the wearer, so the pronoun goes inside the outfit

parts.note: a wally is a fool, British slang, and so is a clot; the 's is kept

explanation.surface: Someone admires a fancy-dress outfit that a man has borrowed from his friend Wally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wally' reads as a name, and is British slang for an idiot, which a clot also is.
explanation.definitionFit: A costume is a set of garments worn together, and garments collectively are what you wear, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Admit daughter every so often sleepily turns over

indicators.note: something turned over ends up the other way round, so the string runs backwards

parts.note: the standard abbreviation in family trees

indicators.note: picking a letter only now and then from the next word means taking every other one

explanation.surface: A parent concedes that their daughter keeps rolling over drowsily in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole string of daughter plus the alternate letters is flipped, which suits a down clue where it is read from the bottom up.
explanation.definitionFit: To yield is to concede or give way, which is the sense of admit as in admitting defeat.

clue.text: One making an impression on you?

definitions.text: One making an impression on you?

parts.words: One making an impression on you?
parts.note: surface reading: someone who wows you on first meeting
setter's reading: literally marking your skin with a lasting design

explanation.walkthrough: 'Making an impression' is an idiom for impressing people, but read literally it is pressing ink into skin, which is what this professional does.
explanation.definitionFit: This artist literally inks permanent designs into a client's skin, a punning take on leaving marks.

clue.text: Jump from raised board, without balancing essentially

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting a word up the grid makes it read backwards
going without something means leaving it out

parts.note: a panel is a flat board

indicators.note: the essence of a word is taken as its very centre letter

parts.note: the middle letter of the nine in balaNcing

explanation.surface: A diver springs from the high board without keeping steady.
explanation.walkthrough: The diving-board picture makes 'raised board' look like the springboard itself; it is a panel written upwards, then its central N dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: To leap is to spring into the air, the direct verb synonym of jump.

clue.text: Pub owner in outskirts of Leatherhead maintaining traditions mostly

indicators.note: most but not all of the word, so its final letter goes
to maintain is to hold, so the outer pair holds the middle pieces
the outskirts of a town are its edges, so take the first and last letters

parts.note: the edges of Leatherhead, a Surrey town
'in' in the sense of 'in addition', plus
lore is traditional knowledge; its last letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A publican on the edge of a Surrey town keeps up old customs, more or less.
explanation.walkthrough: Leatherhead is a commuter town in Surrey. 'In' looks like a placing word but has to supply AND, a loose stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: A landlord in British usage is the licensee who runs a public house, a standard sense of the word.

clue.text: Australia is struck by acclaim for tech company

indicators.note: a name struck from a list is crossed out, so this removes the country from the other word

parts.note: applause is acclaim from an audience

explanation.surface: An Australian firm is hit by a wave of praise for its gadgets.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'struck by' as hit by; the setter means Australia is struck out of the acclaim, leaving a famous fruit-named firm.
explanation.definitionFit: Apple is the Californian maker of iPhones and Mac computers, an example of a technology company.

clue.text: Outfit of Stephen's, emblematic to some extent

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is used, so the answer lies partly within those words

parts.note: running across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Stephen's clothes say something symbolic about him, at least in part.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the apostrophe-s and the start of the next word, so ignore the punctuation.
explanation.definitionFit: An ensemble is a coordinated set of clothes worn together, the fashion sense matching an outfit.

clue.text: Hate swear-word that divides the French

indicators.note: something that divides a word sits inside it, splitting it in two

parts.note: an oath is a curse or profanity

explanation.surface: Someone detests the rude word that splits French speakers into camps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The French' is the regular crossword way to call for LE, LA or LES; here only LE fits around the curse.
explanation.definitionFit: To loathe is to feel intense dislike, a direct verb synonym for hate.

clue.text: During time before shower exercise too much

parts.note: as in 'over the weekend', meaning throughout

explanation.surface: An athlete works out too hard in the minutes before hitting the showers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' just places time ahead of the shower; the shower is weather, not the changing-room kind.
explanation.definitionFit: To overtrain is to push the body with more workouts than it can recover from, the sports term for this.

clue.text: Long introduction to outstanding winter theatre show

parts.note: to long for something is to pant for it

indicators.note: an introduction comes first, so only the opening letter of the next word is used

explanation.surface: A drawn-out opening to a brilliant Christmas-season stage production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' seems an adjective describing the introduction; it is the verb, to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: Pantomime, shortened to panto, is the British family stage comedy staged around Christmas each year.

clue.text: New York banker should regularly start to streamline working

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every second letter of the word is kept
the start of the next word is its first letter only

parts.note: a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: A Manhattan financier ought to begin cutting costs at the office.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'banker' in crosswords is often a river, something with banks; this one flows past New York City.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hudson is the river running past Manhattan, and rivers have banks, hence the cryptic label.

clue.text: Hurriedly leave exam, most quick of all

parts.note: to flee is to run away

explanation.surface: A student bolts from the exam hall faster than everyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma splits the sentence, but the definition is the whole tail phrase, a superlative.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleet means swift of foot, so its superlative describes whoever is swiftest of a group.

clue.text: Top offer, receiving million for book

indicators.note: one letter is received in place of another, a straight swap

parts.note: to submit a proposal is to offer it
the abbreviation for book, the letter that goes

explanation.surface: A publisher's best bid, taking in a million pounds for a book deal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a book auction; in the wordplay B for book is swapped out and M put in its place.
explanation.definitionFit: A summit is the peak or highest point of a mountain, a noun synonym for top.

clue.text: Wood lots use selfishly adult must stop

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a gap, so the pair goes inside the other word

parts.note: to hog is to keep something to yourself

explanation.surface: A telling-off: grown-ups must quit greedily using up so many things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wood lots' reads as woodland plots; the definition is just the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Mahogany is a reddish tropical hardwood prized for furniture, an example of a timber.

clue.text: Snooker venue in Cheshire town Basil's wife mentioned

indicators.note: something mentioned is spoken, so we go by how the names are pronounced

parts.note: Crewe is a railway town in Cheshire, England
Sybil Fawlty, wife of Basil in the TV sitcom Fawlty Towers

explanation.surface: A snooker hall in a Cheshire town that a sitcom character once brought up.
explanation.walkthrough: Basil and Sybil are the hotelier couple in the 1970s British comedy Fawlty Towers. The venue itself is in Sheffield, not Cheshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The Crucible Theatre in Sheffield hosts the World Snooker Championship every spring, so it is the sport's best-known venue.

clue.text: Swimmer from Greece, only failing to finish in medley

indicators.note: not reaching the end means the last letter is missing
a medley is a jumbled mixture, so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: A Greek swimmer who could not complete the medley race at the Olympics.
explanation.walkthrough: The medley is an Olympic swimming event, so the surface makes 'Swimmer' a person; it is a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The conger is a large sea fish of the eel family, and any fish is a creature that swims.

clue.text: Garment king maybe put on one rearing horse

parts.note: a king is one example of a playing card

indicators.note: a horse rearing up rises backwards, and upward in a down clue means read in reverse

parts.note: a nag is an old horse

explanation.surface: A monarch perhaps pulls on a piece of clothing before mounting a horse that rears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King maybe' flags an example: here the king is a playing card, not a ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: A cardigan is a knitted jacket that buttons down the front, an example of an item of clothing.

clue.text: Artist captures a hot Polynesian islander

indicators.note: to capture is to take and hold, so the painter holds the letters

explanation.surface: A painter captures a sultry South Seas native on canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls Gauguin, who painted in Tahiti; the painter needed is Titian.
explanation.definitionFit: Tahiti is the largest island of French Polynesia, so someone born there is a Polynesian islander.

clue.text: Clean trams perhaps?

parts.note: surface reading: someone suggesting a wash for the trams
setter's reading: trams is a smart word going upwards, and smart can mean neat

explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: a synonym of neat, written up the grid in a down entry, spells trams. The question mark flags that trams is only one example of what the phrase could produce.
explanation.definitionFit: To tidy up a room is to put it in order and clean it, a phrasal verb synonym.

clue.text: Name about to visit flipping US city university, incredible!

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside, so these letters enter the others
flipping something over turns it back to front

explanation.surface: An exclamation on the name of an American university city coming up in conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' can pass as a mild British expletive, but here it reverses the city and university together before the name and 'about' go inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Unreal as slang exclaims that something is amazing, just as incredible does.

clue.text: Cheap clothing that's needed for climbing hills?

parts.note: a low price is a cheap one

explanation.surface: Budget outdoor kit that hill walkers need for their climbs.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests hiking kit, but the definition is about cars and bikes.
explanation.definitionFit: Drivers and cyclists shift down to a slow ratio for extra pulling power on steep ascents.

clue.text: Skivvy with physique of a boxer?

definitions.meaning: a skivvy is a menial servant, British slang
a boxer is a breed of dog, so its frame is literally a canine's build

explanation.surface: A lowly servant who happens to have a fighter's build.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxer' looks like a fighter; the question mark says it is the dog breed.
explanation.definitionFit: A dogsbody is British slang for whoever does all the drudge work; split, it is the frame of a canine.

clue.text: Note using revolting English word

indicators.note: revolting means rising up, and rising in a down clue reads backwards

parts.note: a verb is a part of speech, a doing word

explanation.surface: A memo that uses disgusting English language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' passes as disgusting, but means rising in revolt, here upward in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A breve is the long musical note worth two semibreves, an example of a note in notation.

clue.text: Ultimately ignore notice entering cut field

indicators.note: the letters go inside the other word

parts.note: to mow grass is to cut it

indicators.note: what happens ultimately happens at the end, so the last letter is taken

explanation.surface: Eventually disregard the sign posted in a grass field that has been cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut field' reads as a mown field; the definition is the last word alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A meadow is grassland kept for hay, one kind of field in the farming sense.

clue.text: Newspaper Lydia folds

indicators.note: folding reshapes something, so the name's letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Lydia creases up her paper, or perhaps her paper goes out of business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Folds' has two surface readings, a paper being folded or a paper closing down; neither is its job.
explanation.definitionFit: A daily is a paper published every day, noun shorthand for such a publication.

clue.text: Spend change

definitions.meaning: as in moving from one state into another

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spend change' looks like a note about using coins. Both words are verbs: to while away time, and to move from one state into another.
explanation.definitionFit: You pass time by spending it, and water passes from liquid to gas when it changes state.

clue.text: Mean lurcher goes round burying bones

indicators.note: turning round points the string the other way
something buried is concealed inside, here within the phrase

parts.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: A nasty hunting dog circles as it buries bones in the yard.
explanation.walkthrough: A lurcher is a crossbred hunting dog. The dog-and-bone picture makes 'bones' seem literal to the scene, and it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The ulna is one of the two forearm bones, and its Latin plural is used for more than one.

clue.text: Endlessly enraged VIP spread rumour

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter is cut off
the letters are spread about into a new order

explanation.surface: A furious celebrity puts about some gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spread rumour' reads as one action, but 'spread' is the instruction and 'rumour' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The grapevine is the informal chain of gossip, as in hearing it on the grapevine, so it stands for hearsay.

clue.text: Sportsperson presently in Rolls touring area

indicators.note: to tour is to go around, so the mixed letters surround the other piece
rolling tumbles things over, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An athlete is currently being driven around the district in a Rolls-Royce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolls' is dressed as the luxury car brand, capital and all; it is the mixing instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A tennis player is one kind of sportsperson, an example of the general category.
